stories.headline: Cedefop’s new RESET index scores skills in all 244 EU regions
stories.standfirst: Published on 15 October, the regional skills ecosystems index compares regions on skills supply, demand, environment and match. Central Macedonia, home to the Thessaloniki office, ranks 208th; Brussels-Capital ranks 101st.
body: Cedefop describes RESET as the first multidimensional EU regional index focused specifically on skills and VET, with 37 indicators across four dimensions. Scores run from 1 to 100 relative to the other regions (version July 2026, reference year 2024): Stockholm is highest at 75.9, Sud-Vest Oltenia lowest at 26.8. Central Macedonia scores 36.5, fourth of 13 Greek regions; its strongest dimension is skills match (55.3), its weakest skills demand (23.6). Each region also has scores on indicators for people with initial VET: their job tasks, activity, employment and unemployment.
Executive Director Jürgen Siebel said the first event “confirmed how strong the demand is for evidence that reflects territorial realities”.

figure.caption: Chart: Cedefop Daily, from Cedefop’s RESET data (version July 2026, reference year 2024) as published on Apprentix. The dashed line is the median of the 244 regions.

stories.more: RESET: a new Cedefop index scores skills ecosystems in all 244 EU regions.

stories.headline: England plans to charge firms more to train over-25s than young apprentices
stories.standfirst: Ministers are considering raising the cost of training a worker over 25 by 25% under the growth and skills levy, the Guardian reports, to reverse a 40% fall in youth apprenticeship starts over a decade.
body: More than half of new starts are now for over-25s, and under-19 enrolments have almost halved in a decade. The plan adds a “co-investment” rule to the £4bn-a-year levy as part of the response to Alan Milburn’s review of youth unemployment, which, the paper reported a week earlier, will call for a “national pre-apprenticeship route”.

links.text: Apprenticeship starts in England, on Apprentix

stories.more: England: firms may pay more to train over-25s than young apprentices (The Guardian).

stories.headline: 34 apprenticeship schemes show incremental quality gains, Cedefop finds
stories.standfirst: Published on 30 September, five years after Cedefop’s previous analysis of the European framework for quality and effective apprenticeships and ahead of the forthcoming European VET strategy.
body: Criteria on learning and working conditions are usually addressed; on framework conditions the picture is mixed, with several indicators unevenly met. Across criteria, the report finds that where social partners or chambers take a fuller part in decision-making and coordination, they also invest more in implementation, and limited roles go with narrower coverage of quality criteria.
stories.more: Quality of apprenticeships in Europe: Cedefop’s comparison of 34 schemes.

stories.headline: The EU should track AI’s impact on jobs, argues a Social Europe piece
stories.standfirst: Drawing on a June workshop of the European Policy Centre and the Open Markets Institute, it calls for systematic, harmonised EU monitoring of AI’s labour-market impact.
body: Immediate job displacement is not yet visible in aggregate data, it notes, and a job’s estimated AI exposure is often treated as a proxy for displacement risk. The Commission has committed to a high-level expert group tasked with identifying “enhanced analytical tools for monitoring, early warning, foresight and anticipation”, the kind of evidence Cedefop’s skills intelligence produces.
stories.more: Why the EU needs to track AI’s impact on jobs (Social Europe).

stories.headline: Italy and Czechia join Cedefop project on skills for the age of AI
stories.standfirst: WORK.FUTURE, launched in Rome on 22 September, is a two-year project under the EU’s Technical Support Instrument with the Commission’s SG REFORM and both national authorities.
body: Cedefop will analyse up to five occupations or sectors in each country, with foresight workshops and regional roundtables. The newsletter’s comparisons: 26% of employment in both countries was in high-skilled jobs in 2023, against 38% in the EU; adult learning participation was 29% in Italy and 21% in Czechia, against 39%.
stories.more: Italy and Czechia start work with Cedefop on skills for the age of AI.

stories.headline: Early leaving is a process, not an event, says Cedefop policy brief
stories.standfirst: The EU early leaving rate fell to 9.1% in 2025 against a 2030 target of below 8%.
body: The brief sets out 20 intervention approaches covering system capacity, early identification, targeted support and re-engagement, drawing on Cedefop’s VET toolkit for tackling early leaving. Cedefop will launch it at a webinar with the Commission’s DG EAC on 2 December.
stories.more: From risk to resilience: Cedefop’s 20 approaches to early leaving.

stories.headline: Safer jobs can help ease labour shortages, say Cedefop and EU-OSHA
stories.standfirst: A joint article sets EU-OSHA evidence on working conditions beside Cedefop’s intelligence on skills and labour shortages.
body: Shortage occupations it names include welders, electricians, plumbers, cooks, truck drivers and health care assistants, many with demanding or hazardous work. In EU-OSHA’s 2025 OSH Pulse survey, 29% of workers reported stress, anxiety or depression caused or worsened by work, up from 27% in 2022.
stories.more: Cedefop and EU-OSHA: job quality is part of the answer to shortages.

stories.headline: German apprentices report more bullying and violence than students
stories.standfirst: In a Forsa survey for the German Social Accident Insurance, 42% of apprentices had experienced or witnessed insults, against 23% of students.
body: 28% of apprentices knew bullying from experience or observation (students: 12%), and 14% violence or physical assault (students: 3%). Apprentices felt better prepared for safe work: 91% had learned about accident prevention in training, against 53% of students, and 72% felt well or very well prepared for a safe and healthy working life, against 40%. The survey gives no further detail on the violence reported.
stories.more: German apprentices report more bullying and violence than students (DHZ).

stories.headline: Two VET scholars debate the capabilities approach in JVET’s 250th issue
stories.standfirst: Stephanie Allais argues the approach offers VET research little; Leesa Wheelahan argues it has value within broader theories.
body: Allais says its emphasis on human flourishing is important but not new, that it rests on individualism, and that its outcomes-focused stance “gives weak VET systems new ways to fail”. Wheelahan situates it among critical realism, Bernsteinian sociology and Marxism. Allais replies that “compatibility is not a contribution”. Wheelahan, she notes, accepts that the approach cannot say what a curriculum should contain or diagnose labour-market problems; what remains in dispute is whether its vocabulary helps answer VET’s questions or diverts researchers from more specific theories of knowledge, occupations and the conditions of good work.
stories.more: Is the capabilities approach useful for VET research? A JVET debate.

stories.headline: Double mismatch hits graduates hardest, Norwegian survey study finds
stories.standfirst: In the Norwegian Graduate Survey, 90% of those with horizontal mismatch were also overeducated.
body: Studying one form of mismatch without the other overstates its effect: the link between horizontal mismatch and job satisfaction falls by 15% once overeducation is controlled for, and the link between overeducation and satisfaction by 45%. For graduates facing both, the negative effect exceeds that of either alone.
stories.more: Double mismatch: horizontal mismatch and overeducation together hit hardest (Norway).

stories.headline: Swiss apprentices and trainers saw pandemic support differently
stories.standfirst: A mixed-methods study combined a survey of 1,380 vocational trainers with 16 focus groups involving 119 apprentices.
body: Trainers tended to report that workplace support was largely maintained. Apprentices described it as less spontaneous and less consistently accessible, and in firms with more workload more often reported limited guidance, feedback and emotional support.
stories.more: Swiss apprentices and trainers saw workplace support differently in the pandemic.

stories.headline: Training pays off in micro-firms too, Research Policy study finds
stories.standfirst: Using administrative data on training expenses in micro-firms in three Italian regions, the authors find a positive and sizable effect of training on productivity.
body: Firms with fewer than 10 employees are usually lumped in with larger SMEs, the authors note, and some argue training could even hurt their productivity. The effect held across robustness checks and heterogeneity analysis. The paper mentions Cedefop in its full text.
stories.more: Training raises productivity in micro-firms (Research Policy).

stories.headline: Germany’s minimum apprentice pay rises to €764 in 2027
stories.standfirst: For apprenticeships starting in 2027, the legal minimum rises to €764 a month in the first year, up 5.6% on 2026.
body: Germany has had fewer apprentices than it needs for years, the paper notes, and the minimum, in law since 2020, is meant to help turn that round. Where a collective agreement exists, its rate applies. BIBB updates the amount each year.
stories.more: Germany: minimum apprentice pay rises to €764 in 2027 (DHZ).

stories.headline: Spain’s private training providers push back against a draft VET decree
stories.standfirst: ACADE, the association of private schools, says the draft royal decree on vocational training limits the opening of private centres and online provision.
body: Its president argued that measures presented as quality improvements target private centres while leaving out public ones, and asked for the draft to be halted, Magisterio reports. ACADE says private VET has grown with demand from students, families and employers.
stories.more: Spain: private providers push back against the draft VET decree (Magisterio).

stories.headline: Greece lets 257 small apprenticeship-year classes run this year
stories.standfirst: The Ministry of Education has allowed 257 classes of the post-secondary apprenticeship year to run in 2026–2027 with fewer apprentices than its regulation sets.
body: Staffing is tight elsewhere: in the Cyclades, the local secondary teachers’ union says 130 teaching posts are still empty a month into term, and ESOS reports a new vocational upper-secondary school running with its director as its only teacher.

links.text: The post-secondary apprenticeship year, on Apprentix

stories.more: Greece: 257 small apprenticeship-year classes allowed to run (ESOS).

stories.headline: AI literacy is a new basic skill, inter-agency report argues
stories.standfirst: Written within the Inter-agency TVET group on skill mismatch in digitalised labour markets, with inputs from Cedefop.
body: It finds AI adoption raising demand for higher-order cognitive and socioemotional skills and for digital and data science skills, and a small but fast-growing market for jobs building and maintaining AI systems. Everyone now needs the ability to use AI tools safely and ethically, it argues, and skills policies should prioritise broad capabilities and human agency.

links.text: Changing landscape of skills in the age of AI

stories.more: Changing landscape of skills in the age of AI: inter-agency report with Cedefop.

stories.headline: How VET and business work together: a new Cedefop Insight
stories.standfirst: Drawing on the Timeline of VET policies in the EU-27, Iceland and Norway, it finds cooperation moving beyond work placements.
body: VET-business cooperation now also covers skills foresight, governance, teacher training and entrepreneurship education. Examples include France’s Campus of Excellence Industry of the Future South and Spain’s Digitalízate, where 58% of certification completers are women. It says SMEs need brokers such as chambers and sector bodies.

links.text: Policy approaches to strengthening VET-business partnerships

stories.more: Cedefop Insight: how countries build VET-business partnerships.

stories.headline: Policy pointers for Estonia’s skills forecasting system published
stories.standfirst: The report, dated 13 October, comes from a project run with Estonia’s Ministry of Education and Research and the Commission.
body: Based on desk research, consultations, peer learning and examples from other countries, it sets strategic directions for OSKA and Estonia’s wider skills governance, “intentionally indicative rather than prescriptive”, and may inspire other countries with similar reform plans.
stories.more: Policy pointers for Estonia’s skills anticipation system (Cedefop).

stories.headline: EU employment and social policy ministers meet in the Council today
stories.standfirst: The Council’s media advisory lists the agenda, timing and public sessions of Monday’s Employment, Social Policy, Health and Consumer Affairs Council (EPSCO).
stories.more: EPSCO: employment and social policy ministers meet today.

stories.headline: Quality jobs best way out of poverty for those who can work, says Mînzatu
stories.standfirst: Ahead of the International Day for the Eradication of Poverty, the Executive Vice-President said one in five Europeans is at risk of poverty and social exclusion.
body: The economy “cannot afford leaving almost 50 million people outside the labour market”, she said, pointing to a first-stage consultation of the social partners, launched in July, on EU action for people facing significant barriers to work.
stories.more: Mînzatu: quality jobs are the best way out of poverty for those who can work.

stories.headline: Greek minister brings AI and vocational training to informal EU meeting
stories.standfirst: At the informal meeting of EU education ministers in Dublin on 15–16 October, Greece’s education minister spoke on AI in education and upgrading vocational training, ESOS reports.
body: Her other themes were the new lyceum, a national diploma and tackling educational inequalities.
stories.more: Informal EU education ministers’ meeting in Dublin: Greece on AI and VET (ESOS).

stories.headline: Cooperation is key to AI-age skills, ETF says after WorldSkills
stories.standfirst: An ETF delegation led by director Pilvi Torsti joined the Commission delegation at WorldSkills 2026 in Shanghai, 21–27 September.
body: The ETF attended as a partner in the German-led Towards a Global TVET Agenda initiative and held talks with India’s Ministry for Skill Development and Entrepreneurship ahead of the India-EU High-Level Dialogue.
stories.more: ETF at WorldSkills 2026: international cooperation on AI-age skills.

stories.headline: Irish tech union grows five-fold amid AI-driven layoffs
stories.standfirst: While Dublin hosted the presidency’s International AI Summit, a Workers’ AI Counter Summit met the weekend before, Politico Europe reports.
body: The Digital and Techworker Alliance, founded in 2023, had around 270 members in its first year and a half and now has more than 1,350, its organiser told the outlet. Ireland counts more than 170,000 tech workers; Meta has roughly halved its Irish workforce since the pandemic, and TikTok plans to cut around 300 Irish jobs, mostly in trust and safety. An IMF report this year found Ireland’s labour market “relatively more exposed” to AI than many advanced economies.
stories.more: Irish tech workers unionise as AI-driven layoffs spread (Politico Europe).

stories.headline: Losing a job in a carbon-intensive sector costs more, German data show
stories.standfirst: Displaced workers from high-carbon sectors face larger earnings and wage losses than others, a VoxEU column finds from administrative data.
body: These sectors are regionally concentrated and involve specific occupations and tasks with high firm-wage premia, the authors write, which narrows workers’ options for jobs with similar skills and pay.
stories.more: Green transition: job loss costs more in carbon-intensive sectors (VoxEU).

stories.headline: Resilience buffers burnout among German VET teachers, study finds
stories.standfirst: A survey of 1,470 vocational teachers found task scope and complexity to be the most prevalent job demands.
body: Demands were linked to lower well-being and job satisfaction and more burnout; of the resources studied, only resilience moderated the effect on burnout. The authors suggest reducing demands and building resilience in teacher training.
stories.more: German VET teachers: resilience buffers burnout (ERVET).

stories.headline: Is overeducation lower in green industries? It depends on the measure
stories.standfirst: Using PIAAC data for seven Central and Eastern European countries and Cedefop’s 2019 framework for green industries.
body: Workers’ own assessments show no difference between green and other industries; the statistical measure finds less overeducation in green industries. The authors urge caution, given the broad definition of green industries.
stories.more: Overeducation in green industries depends on how it is measured (DIEM).

stories.headline: New apprenticeship policies in Cedefop’s 2025 timeline update
stories.standfirst: First reported in the 2025 update by Cedefop and ReferNet, as summarised on Apprentix.
body: They include Denmark’s substantial reinforcement of VET and mandatory work experience, Greece’s 2025–2027 strategic plan for VET, lifelong learning and youth, Slovakia’s tertiary VET reinforcement and Slovenia’s programme document for development planning until 2033.
stories.more: New apprenticeship policies in Cedefop’s 2025 timeline update.

stories.headline: Vienna debates how young people find a way into apprenticeships
stories.standfirst: At the Tag der Wiener Jugend, experts discussed the difficult search for apprenticeships and the falling number of training companies, Der Standard reports.
body: The head of Austria’s public employment service, AMS, told the event he is interested in applicants who have changed course.
stories.more: Vienna: experts on young people’s hard search for apprenticeships (Der Standard).

stories.headline: Cedefop describes Ireland’s further education and training system
stories.standfirst: A new short description covers VET for learners aged 16+ and adults, delivered mainly through 16 education and training boards.
body: It highlights the dual apprenticeship model, tertiary degrees linking further and higher education, and microqualifications under the Skills to Advance initiative.
stories.more: VET in Ireland: Cedefop short description and Spotlight.

stories.headline: Agency board changes for Cedefop, Eurofound and EU-OSHA
stories.standfirst: The Council replaced a member of Cedefop’s Management Board for Bulgaria (decision of 24 September).
body: It also replaced a member and an alternate for Denmark at Eurofound (9 October) and members for Estonia and Cyprus at EU-OSHA (1 October).
stories.more: Board changes at Cedefop, Eurofound and EU-OSHA (Official Journal).

stories.headline: EU leaders and social partners meet at the Tripartite Social Summit
stories.standfirst: The twice-yearly summit brought EU leaders and social partners together in Brussels on 14 October.
stories.more: Tripartite Social Summit, 14 October: EU leaders and social partners.

stories.headline: ELA brings seven countries together on disguised job placement
stories.standfirst: Authorities from Belgium, Czechia, Germany, the Netherlands, Lithuania, Slovakia and Finland met in Prague on 6–7 October.
body: An ELA study on temporary work agencies and other forms of employment intermediation is expected in early 2027.
stories.more: ELA: seven countries compare tools against disguised job placement.

stories.headline: Teachers and trainers are key agents of change, says the ETF
stories.standfirst: As AI and the green transition reshape labour markets, the ETF argues for investing in the educators who support young people and adults throughout their learning.
stories.more: ETF: why investing in teachers and trainers matters.

stories.headline: In AI hub Montreal, young graduates weigh chances against fears
stories.standfirst: Some students and newcomers expect new opportunities; others fear their skills will soon be outdated, Le Monde reports (subscription).
stories.more: Montreal’s young graduates and AI (Le Monde, subscription).

stories.headline: Nine VETNET papers from ECER 2026 mention Cedefop
stories.standfirst: Published on 13 October in the VETNET Conference Series.
body: They include studies of AI-mediated vocational pedagogy, embodied AI role-play in extended reality for retail apprentices, and an inclusive VET ecosystem.
stories.more: Nine VETNET conference papers mention Cedefop.

stories.headline: Chile’s TVET schools turn one internship policy into many
stories.standfirst: Interviews with 37 internship coordinators show schools reading the policy either as competency validation or as a route to employability.
body: Those readings shape which students go to which workplaces; engaging employers is a recurring barrier.
stories.more: Chile: how TVET schools enact internship policy (Education + Training).

stories.headline: HR professionals see AI reshaping their roles more than taking jobs
stories.standfirst: Their insecurity is mostly about changing role expectations rather than job loss, and self-directed workplace learning helps them regain agency.
stories.more: AI and HR professionals: workplace learning as a buffer (Journal of Workplace Learning).

stories.headline: Teaching in Swedish prisons is a practice of its own, study finds
stories.standfirst: Interviews with 14 adult educators in Swedish prisons show a pedagogy built on trust, responsibility and empowerment.
body: Prison education is not simply adult education delivered under constraints, the authors argue, but a practice of its own, shaped by institutional rules, security routines and students’ varied educational backgrounds, and aimed at the students’ holistic development. It is negotiated between care and control, autonomy and coercion, trust and vigilance.
stories.more: Adult education in Swedish prisons (International Journal of Lifelong Education).

stories.headline: From the archive: how qualifications govern access to occupations
stories.standfirst: A Cedefop study dated 18 October 2013.
body: Qualifications define what a person needs to know and be able to do to carry out an activity on the labour market. Health and safety, consumer protection and quality assurance are quoted to justify them, but they may also defend the private interests of professional groups, the study notes.
stories.more: From the archive (2013): the role of qualifications in governing occupations.

stories.headline: From the archive: tracking digital skill needs in online job ads
stories.standfirst: A Cedefop policy brief dated 20 October 2023.
body: Using Cedefop analysis of online job advertisements, it showed the demand for digital skills across the EU-27 and argued for faster implementation of digital policy and for up- and reskilling.
stories.more: From the archive (2023): Going digital means skilling for digital.

lives.headline: Germany’s first carpentry world champion, 1967, still in the workshop at 78
lives.standfirst: He won gold at the forerunner of WorldSkills in Madrid at 18, ran the family firm for decades and trained most of its staff himself.
body: In July 1967, Albert Baumann beat young carpenters from Korea, the Netherlands, Ireland, Japan, Great Britain and Switzerland. He had begun his apprenticeship in the family firm in Flein in 1964; for the national final in Berlin he took a plane for the first time, his big carpenter’s saw stowed behind the back row. He became a master carpenter in 1970, took over the business, trained most of its up to twelve employees and handed it to his children in 2012. At 78 he still works in the workshop.
long: Albert Baumann grew up in a carpentry firm in Flein that his grandfather founded in 1896; as a child, he says, he was already working with a fretsaw. He began his apprenticeship in the family firm in 1964 and finished first at every level of the trade competitions, from guild to chamber to state. In 1966 he flew for the first time, to the national final in Berlin, his big carpenter’s saw stowed behind the back row on the airport staff’s advice. He won there too, at 18, and was honoured by the Federal President.

In July 1967 the German team went by coach from Duisburg to Madrid for the 16th International Vocational Training Competition, the forerunner of WorldSkills. The task was a hipped roof for a building with an extension, in three days. He finished first, after two, and used the spare time for sightseeing; he still talks about the Prado. On 17 July he took gold, ahead of young carpenters from Korea, the Netherlands, Ireland, Japan, Great Britain and Switzerland. Back in Flein, he recalls, customers came by to congratulate him, and some joked that prices would now go up, with a world champion in the workshop.

He qualified as a master carpenter in 1970 and took over the business from his father three years later. At its peak it employed twelve people, most of whom he had trained himself, and for decades he volunteered for the trade’s young people in the local carpenters’ guild. In 2012 he handed the firm to his children, the fourth generation. At 78 he still works in the workshop. Since 1967, four more German carpenters have won world gold, in 1973, 2003, 2015 and 2019.

lives.headline: What world gold cost a young cabinetmaker
lives.standfirst: Tobias Kelz won WorldSkills gold in Shanghai by a single point, finishing his piece in the last second.
body: He had 22 hours to build a piece of furniture he first saw on day one, and made two careless mistakes along the way. The road began after his journeyman’s exam: chamber, Bavarian and national titles, then a year of training with the other winners. In the last six months there was no free time, he says: work by day, the workshop after hours. Some days he asked himself why he was doing it. He would do it again, he says, but not a second time.
long: He had 22 hours to build a piece of furniture he first saw on day one, with solid wood, panels, veneer and doors to hang, and made two careless mistakes along the way; his trainer, whom he could only consult in breaks, found a way to recover. In the evenings they negotiated every minute of the next day’s time.

The road began after his journeyman’s exam, more than two years earlier: the chamber, Bavarian and national competitions, then a year of training with the other national winners before the trainers picked two cabinetmakers for Shanghai. In the last six months there was no real free time: a week a month at the wood technical school in Bad Wildungen, work by day, the workshop after hours. Some days, he says, he asked himself why he was doing it; his employer accepted many absences.
What he takes away: new techniques, more speed, and more calm. He would do it again, he says, but not a second time.

lives.headline: A class for teenagers left without a school place: one teacher’s diary
lives.standfirst: In a vocational lycée in Seine-Saint-Denis, a history and geography teacher is starting a class for students who left lower secondary with nowhere to go.
body: On 1 September the first names arrived, and worried families came early to the interviews. Mathilde Ouguel’s class takes at most 30 students, with a school day from 10 in the morning, core lessons before lunch, workshops after and six to eight weeks of placements. On the first morning everyone was on time. Asked what they had understood of the project, one student said the teachers believe in them and want to get them out of where they are. On 11 September, 13 more students arrived.

lives.headline: Preston’s AI bootcamp offers young people out of work an apprenticeship
lives.standfirst: A three-week pilot for 16- to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training ends with an offer of AI apprenticeships.
body: In a youth centre opposite Preston bus station, five young people at laptops learn why AI models need clean data. The pilot, open to 70 people, links to apprenticeships with partners including JD Sports, Heinz and Agilysys, in AI marketing or IT helpdesks. Khudeija Rafique, 18, from Burnley, says it would be “really helpful with whatever job I would like to go into”. A 17-year-old says the course changed his opinion of AI. A King’s College London researcher says little is yet known about how AI affects non-graduate work.

lives.headline: German concrete builders win world gold after training around their jobs
lives.standfirst: Jakob Distler and Tim Arnold beat eight teams in concrete construction at WorldSkills 2026 in Shanghai.
body: Four days at their physical limit, they told the Deutsche Handwerks Zeitung; when the concrete for a staircase came out far too liquid, they formed a lid over the step and still finished on time. They trained from April, every two to three weeks with their national trainer in Nördlingen and on evenings at home, with their bosses giving them the time. Their Chinese rivals, they observed, train for years. Now, they say, they pass their enthusiasm for the trade on to the new apprentices.

2026-10-19.headline: The ETF’s future is open for feedback until 13 November
2026-10-19.standfirst: The Commission is collecting views on strengthening and modernising the European Training Foundation, Cedefop’s sister agency. Four other initiatives open for feedback touch training, AI or labour mobility.

2026-10-20.headline: Three Chinese counties, three ways to govern vocational training
2026-10-20.standfirst: A comparative study of Longkou, Zhucheng and Pingyi in Shandong finds that local conditions, not national institutions alone, shape how governments, schools and employers organise skill formation.

parts.label: The question
parts.text: How do uneven local development conditions shape the way vocational education and training is governed within one country?

parts.label: How it was studied
parts.text: Comparative case studies of three counties in Shandong Province, treating governance as a configuration of authority, resources, coordination and educational provision.

parts.label: What it found
parts.text: Three locally embedded configurations: integrated governance, platform-mediated governance and service-network governance. They differ in how governments, schools and employers coordinate resources and connect educational opportunities with labour markets.

parts.label: The caveat
parts.text: Three counties in one province, and an account of how governance is organised rather than of its results for learners.

parts.label: Why read it
parts.text: Research on skill formation usually compares national systems. The paper argues that local capacity, institutional history and labour mobility shape it within countries too: the regional lens of Cedefop’s RESET index.

2026-10-21.headline: France: a million apprentices, and the first fall in a decade
2026-10-21.standfirst: Apprentices under contract grew 2.4-fold from December 2017, to 1,014,485 at the end of 2025, but fell 3% over the year: the first annual fall since December 2015.
body: Much of the growth was in higher education: 62% of France’s apprentices now prepare a higher-education diploma, up from 39% at the end of 2017. France has two schemes in Cedefop’s database: the apprenticeship contract, where apprentices are most likely between 18 and 24, and the professionalisation contract, where many are over 24.

2026-10-22.headline: Learning about AI left hospital trainers less sure of themselves
2026-10-22.standfirst: A study at Montreal’s university hospital describes a “knowing-doing gap”: awareness of AI tools grew faster than their use.

parts.label: What happened
parts.text: Six healthcare professionals who train colleagues at the Centre hospitalier de l’Université de Montréal followed an eight-week programme of pedagogical guides and microlearning videos on AI, then discussed it in two focus groups.

parts.label: What they found
parts.text: More knowledge came with less confidence. Participants drew lines between appropriate and inappropriate uses of AI, and tool access, protected time and institutional endorsement shaped how far their AI literacy developed.

parts.label: What it means for skills
parts.text: The authors read lower confidence as a sign of more differentiated professional judgment rather than failure, and argue that individual learning needs an infrastructure of agency. Their findings, they write, challenge adoption-centric models of AI literacy.

2026-10-23.headline: When 764 VET experts went to learn from each other abroad
2026-10-23.standfirst: Cedefop’s review of the 2007 study visits programme counted 59 visits on 11 themes, for VET specialists, policy-makers and social partners.
body: Themes included making vocational training more attractive for young people and adult learners, and developing entrepreneurship. Questionnaires from 2005 and 2006 were analysed for what the visits changed in participants’ organisations and work.

parts.label: Since then
parts.text: Mobility is now measured for learners too: in 2023, 5.3% of EU vocational learners spent at least 10 days abroad (today’s chart). Germany has the most Erasmus-accredited VET organisations, 692, ahead of France with 516.

2026-10-19.headline: Recent VET graduates in work: the EU at 80.1%, short of its 82% target
reading: In 2025, 80.1% of 20–34-year-olds who had finished vocational upper-secondary or post-secondary education one to three years earlier were in work, up from 75.9% in 2020. The EU target was at least 82% by 2025.
Germany led with 91.5%. Belgium stood at 75.4%, and Greece, at 58.0%, was lowest among the countries with data.

2026-10-20.headline: Do workers’ skills match their jobs? 57% say yes
reading: In 2024, 57% of EU workers answered “My present skills correspond well with my duties”, the same as in 2015 and up from 55% in 2010. The others said they needed further training, or could cope with more demanding duties.
Malta (77%) and Portugal (76%) were highest, Austria lowest (37%); Belgium and Greece were both at 61%.

2026-10-21.headline: Apprentices in France, December of each year since 2013
reading: The number more than doubled from 425,876 in December 2017 to a peak of 1,048,840 in December 2024, then fell to 1,014,485 a year later.
Mid-year figures are lower: 911,425 in July 2026, against 944,260 in July 2025.

2026-10-22.headline: Six in ten EU adults have at least basic digital skills
reading: In 2025, 60.4% of 16–74-year-olds in the EU had at least basic digital skills, up from 53.9% in 2021: the ground on which any AI literacy has to be built.
The Netherlands (83.6%) and Ireland (82.8%) led; Romania was lowest (31.8%). Belgium stood at 61.2%.

2026-10-23.headline: Learning abroad: 5.3% of EU vocational learners in 2023
reading: Mobile IVET learners, those with at least 10 days abroad, as a share of a cohort of IVET graduates: 3.6% in 2018, 4.1% in 2019, just over 1% in 2020 and 5.3% in 2023.

0.question: What share of adults aged 25–64 in the EU took part in education or training in the last four weeks, in 2025?
0.answer: Up from 10.1% in 2015, with a dip to 9.1% in 2020.
